For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

=== key 6ccdc032f78a

Write-up text before the decision: pute/comments](/api/post/compute-trends-comparison-to-openai-s-ai-and-compute/comments) * Post URL (Markdown, compact): [/api/post/compute-trends-comparison-to-openai-s-ai-and-compute?compact=1](/api/post/compute-trends-comparison-to-openai-s-ai-and-compute?compact=1) This is a slightly modified version of Appendix E from our paper "*Compute Trends Across Three Eras of Machine Learning*". You can find the summary [here](/api/post/XKtybmbjhC6mXDm5z) and the complete paper [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05924). After sharing our updated compute trends analysis a common question was: "*So how are your findings different from* [*OpenAI’s previous compute analysis*](https://openai.com/blog/ai-and-compute/) *by Amodei and Hernandez?*". We try to answer this question in this short post. Comparison to OpenAI’s AI and Compute ------------------------------------- [OpenAI’s analysis](https://openai.com/blog/ai-and-compute/) shows a 3.4 month doubling from 2012 to 2018. Our analysis suggests a 5.7 month doubling time from 2012 to 2022 (Table 1, *purple*). In this post, we investigate this difference. We use the same methods for estimating compute for the final training run. Our methods are described in detail in [*Estimating training compute of Deep Learning models*](/api/post/HvqQm6o8KnwxbdmhZ). Our analysis differs in three points: (I) number of samples, (II) extended time period, and (III) the identification of a distinct large-scale trend. Of these, either the time period or the separation of the large-scale models is enough to explain the difference between our results.

=== key 9e5320c291ce
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect

Write-up text before the decision: [2105.03109] Laplace Matching for fast Approximate Inference in Latent Gaussian Models -- # Computer Science Machine Learning arXiv:2105.03109 (cs) [Submitted on 7 May 2021 (v1), last revised 11 Oct 2022 (this version, v2)] # Title:Laplace Matching for fast Approximate Inference in Latent Gaussian Models View PDF > Abstract:Bayesian inference on non-Gaussian data is often non-analytic and requires computationally expensive approximations such as sampling or variational inference. [...] The concept, which we call Laplace Matching, involves closed-form, approximate, bi-directional transformations between the parameter spaces of exponential families. These are constructed from Laplace approximations under custom-designed basis transformations. The mappings can then be leveraged to effectively turn a latent Gaussian distribution into an approximate conjugate prior to a rich class of observable variables. This allows us to train latent Gaussian models such as Gaussian Processes on non-Gaussian data at nearly no additional cost. The method can be thought of as a pre-processing step which can be implemented in <5 lines of code and runs in less than a second. Furthermore, Laplace Matching yields a simple way to group similar data points together, e.g. to produce inducing points for GPs.

Write-up text before the decision: 4.2 Comparison to alternative methods We compare our mainline probe to several alternatives, including a black-box baseline (Figure 6). Further results for each experiment are included in Appendix B. Figure 6: Comparison of various probe-training datasets and methodologies, as well as a black-box baseline. We our probe trained on the Instructed-Pairs dataset (“pretend to be an honest/deceptive person…”), to three probes trained on honest and deceptive responses from our Roleplaying dataset. One of these probes uses the raw activations, one uses SAE activations, and one uses the activations after a consistent followup question (“Are you being deceptive?” “No”). Finally we compare to a probe fit to the difference in activation between two responses to a single question and a black-box baseline where GPT 4o classifies entire transcripts as deceptive or honest. Top: AUROC of classifiers distinguishing deceptive and honest answers to each dataset. Bottom: Recall (TPR on deceptive) for 1% FPR on our control responses. ##### Train on Roleplaying. Instead of training on the Instructed-Pairs dataset we train a probe to distinguish between honest and deceptive responses on the Roleplaying dataset. This probe perfectly separates the held-out roleplaying examples. It generalizes slightly better to Insider Trading Report, but significantly worse on Sandbagging. One potential explanation is that the Instructed-Pairs and Sandbagging datasets both involve instructing the model to lie, giving a smaller generalization gap between those datasets than between Roleplaying and Sandbagging.

We test several different alternatives for fitting linear probes: - • Logistic Regression, as in our mainline experiments - • Difference of Means. We take the direction $\mu_{\text{deceptive}}-\mu_{\text{honest}}$, where these are the mean activations on deceptive and honest token positions in our training dataset. - • LDA (Linear Discriminant Analysis). We take the direction $\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_{\text{deceptive}}-\mu_{\text{honest}})$, where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of the centred dataset. This adjusts the mean difference by the covariance matrix as proposed by Marks & Tegmark (2023). - • LAT (Linear Artificial Tomography), as in Zou et al. (2023). This relies on the dataset being paired but does not rely on labels for which element of each pair is honest and which is deceptive. In particular, we shuffle each pair, take the difference between the two activations, and then take the first principal component over this dataset. We compare the performance of these methods in Figure 11. Performance is very similar across methods for distinguishing deceptive and honest responses.
